title: Iraq oil smuggling clampdown threatens ties with Kurds, Iran
description: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi's crackdown on oil smuggling is garnering praise from the US but risks straining relations with Iraq's Kurds and Iran. By aiming to centralize control over oil resources and border crossings, Zaidi seeks to assert state authority and combat corruption, which the US supports in its effort to counter Iran's influence and secure investments in Iraq. However, this move has sparked tensions with Kurdish authorities, who fear a threat to their autonomy.
text: BAGHDAD: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi is taking bold steps to curb rampant oil smuggling, moves that the US has praised but that risk putting him at odds with Iraq’s Kurds and neighboring Iran.
Iraq has long been stuck balancing the competing influence of the United States and Iran. But Zaidi has been steering the country closer to Washington and has been lauded by President Donald Trump.

On Friday, Trump said he backs Zaidi’s “efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state.”
Zaidi, who has repeatedly vowed to disarm Iran-backed armed groups, recently went after a powerful faction over alleged oil smuggling.

On Tuesday, he also moved to place the Kurdistan region’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control — a step that would tighten Baghdad’s grip on the autonomous region while cutting smuggling routes into Iran.

Zaidi enjoys close ties with Trump envoy Tom Barrack, who is driving efforts to expand US oil investments in Iraq and develop an export route through Syria that could reduce the dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
Yet the US must first deal with two main challenges: Iran-backed groups hostile to its interests, and rampant smuggling that gives a lifeline to Iran and threatens investments.

The US, which is intensifying its economic pressure against the Islamic republic, accuses Tehran of using Iraq to evade sanctions, and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals and companies for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.
Sajad Jiyad, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said that Zaidi’s “strategy is aligned with what America wants for Iraq and for its Iran policy.”

“A stronger central government serves US interests better,” as it can better control the country and rein in armed groups, even if that weakens traditional US allies such as the Kurdistan authorities, the Baghdad-based analyst said.

Zaidi’s crackdown on oil smuggling through Kurdistan targets routes used to move crude into Iran where it is being blended with Iranian crude for export, according to an intelligence document cited by Iraq’s state media.
Cutting off that flow is “exactly what US policy is right now: maximum pressure through economic blockade,” Jiyad said.
Earlier this month, Zaidi went after Kataeb Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed group that refuses to give up its weapons, over alleged oil smuggling in its stronghold south of Baghdad.
He later sent government forces into the area under a compromise deal that averted a confrontation.
Several Iraqi political sources told AFP that Zaidi’s relationship with Tehran has strained and that Iran will not accept that its allied factions disarm amid a regional war.
Zaidi’s decision to put Kurdistan’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control sparked angry reactions from Kurdish authorities.
Relations between Baghdad and Irbil, the capital of Kurdistan, have long been tense, with recurring disputes over territories, oil exports or budget allocations.
Iraq’s Kurds, who have close ties with the US, have repeatedly warned of federal government attempts to undermine their autonomy, which was formalized by Iraq’s 2005 constitution.
They have become more wary recently seeing that US policy in Syria has denied the Kurds there autonomy in favor of centralized authority in Damascus.

Irbil-based political analyst Lawk Ghafuri said that the Kurds will consider Zaidi’s decision a “threat,” but they will eventually strike a deal, adding that Zaidi’s strategy is to rise the stakes enough to secure concessions.
Judiciary chief Faeq Zaidan, widely seen as close to Zaidi, has called for a dialogue next week to diffuse tensions.
At its core, Zaidi’s goal is to rein in armed groups, assert greater control over oil wealth and draw foreign investment, Ghafuri said.
The Middle East war and the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz dealt a blow to Iraq’s oil exports, which make up 90 percent of its revenues.
The US has also slowed cash shipments for Iraq’s oil sales, handled by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York since 2003.
Government spokesperson Haidar Al-Aboudi told state media that Iraq’s losses due to oil smuggling from Kurdistan exceeded $100 billion between 2008 to 2025.
Kurdish authorities used to export oil independently, without the approval of the federal government, which has consistently insisted that all oil exports fall under its authority.
Jiyad said Iraq is facing a big deficit, and Zaidi is also “trying to find ways to increase public revenues and one of those is to stop” losing money to oil smuggling.
